{
  "persuasion": "PERSUADED",
  "support_scope": "FULL",
  "rationale": "The book's core identification—that 'works' names deeds/actions (not a synonym for obedience) and that context alone decides whether a given deed executes a legitimate command, conflicts with God's command, or is offered for wages—best accounts for the printed references and the method-driven cross-text evidence. The common interpretation's primary framing of works as fruit/evidence of inner faith (or as a soteriological cipher for law-works or self-righteous effort) is not contradicted but is secondary: it presupposes the deed-level referent the book establishes and then layers additional theological freight. The book preserves the distinctions required by Romans 4 (laborer claiming debt) versus James 2 (Abraham's faith made visible) and Luke 17 (even complete obedience remains duty, not wage), while Exodus 18:20 supplies the definitional first use (ordinances, way walked, work done). No supplied text requires the common reading as the primary lexical identification; the book's reading explains all of them with fewer unsupported steps.",
  "book_core_identification": "Works = deeds/actions (not a synonym for obedience); a work becomes obedience only when it executes a legitimate command and becomes disobedience when the command or deed conflicts with God's; Romans 4 uses the laborer's work offered for wages/debt while James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible; complete obedience still earns no wage because the servant has only done his duty.",
  "book_secondary_elaborations": [
    "Definition first fixed at Exodus 18:20 (ordinances taught, way walked, work done).",
    "Psalm 111:7 pairing of God's works with his sure commandments.",
    "Micah 6:16 as illustration of evil works under rival statutes.",
    "Works can be 'kept' (Revelation 2:26) because they are commandment-shaped.",
    "Cross-references to the treatment of faith/works in the Knowing-Faith-Love chapter and the full Paul vocabulary study in The End of the Law.",
    "Uniform symbolic-language method (OT pattern attestation before NT usage)."
  ],
  "strongest_counter_interpretation": "The mainstream Christian consensus that 'works' primarily denotes the outward deeds that function as fruit/evidence of an inward spiritual state (good works as the necessary fruit of genuine faith/grace; evil works as the fruit of flesh/unbelief), with the further Protestant refinement that they are never the meritorious ground of justification, and the frequent polemical shorthand that 'works' (especially 'works of the law') stands for self-righteous human effort or legalism opposed to grace.",
  "counter_core_identification": "Works = outward moral deeds that evidence/reveal the heart (good works as fruit of faith; evil works as fruit of the flesh), assessed at judgment and sharply distinguished from the faith that alone justifies.",
  "counter_relation_to_book_core": "SAME_CORE_BROADER",
  "material_core_denial": "The counter does not deny that works are deeds; it adds the further claim that the primary theological force of the term is evidential/fruit-bearing (or, in some usages, a cipher for legalistic effort), thereby treating the book's deed-vs-obedience and wage-vs-duty distinctions as secondary or already subsumed.",
  "counter_case": [
    "Ephesians 2:8-10 pairs 'not of works' with 'created ... for good works,' classically read as fruit of grace.",
    "James 2:14-26 and Matthew 7:16-20 treat works as the visible proof that faith is living.",
    "Romans 3:28 / Galatians 2:16 and Romans 4:4-5 are routinely read as excluding works (or works of the law) from justification, making 'works' the rival of faith.",
    "Revelation 20:12-13 and Matthew 16:27 make works the basis of judgment, reinforcing their role as evidence of the person.",
    "The New Perspective and Catholic/Orthodox readings further specialize the term without abandoning the deed-level sense."
  ],
  "book_explanatory_advantages": [
    "Explains why Romans 4 can treat 'worketh' as wage-claim while James 2 treats Abraham's works as faith made perfect without contradiction: the term itself is simply 'deed'; context supplies the master and the claim.",
    "Accounts for Luke 17:7-10 (even total obedience remains duty, never surplus wage) as a direct definition of the economic relation the book isolates.",
    "Preserves Exodus 18:20 as the plain definitional locus (work = the deed that must be done once the way is shown) rather than retrofitting a soteriological metaphor.",
    "Keeps Micah 6:16 and Psalm 111:7 as ordinary illustrations of deeds under rival or divine statutes, without forcing every occurrence into a faith-vs-works binary.",
    "Avoids collapsing 'works' into either 'obedience' or 'legalism,' which the common reading frequently does in popular usage."
  ],
  "counter_explanatory_advantages": [
    "Captures the dominant pastoral and confessional use of 'works' language across Protestant, Catholic, and Orthodox traditions.",
    "Efficiently organizes the large body of judgment and fruit texts (Matthew 7, Revelation 2-3, Galatians 5) under a single fruit/evidence heading.",
    "Explains why 'not of works' can function as a theological slogan against merit without needing the book's finer wage-duty distinction in every sermon."
  ],
  "evidence_book_core_cannot_explain": [],
  "comparative_winner": "BOOK",
  "decisive_sources": [
    "Exodus 18:20 (definitional first teaching of 'the work that they must do')",
    "Luke 17:7-10 (complete obedience remains duty, no wage owed)",
    "Romans 4:4-5 (work offered for debt vs. faith counted as righteousness)",
    "James 2:21-22 (Abraham's works as faith made perfect/visible)",
    "Psalm 111:7 (works of his hands paired with sure commandments)",
    "Micah 6:16 (works of the house of Ahab under rival statutes)"
  ],
  "unresolved_objections": [
    "The book does not itself supply a full catalog of every NT occurrence of 'works of the law,' leaving some room for New Perspective or traditional readings of those specialized phrases.",
    "Pastoral and confessional traditions will continue to treat the fruit/evidence layer as primary even if the lexical core is conceded.",
    "The entry's cross-reference to The End of the Law is necessary for a complete treatment of Paul's vocabulary, so the present entry alone is not exhaustive on Pauline usage."
  ],
  "confidence": "high"
}
